paras: The lynching of George Scott took place at Brazil, Indiana, on the night of December 11-12, 1880, when masked men took him from the jail and hanged him. Scott, described in the press as "a half-breed Indian and negro," was held on an accusation of assaulting Mrs. Allison, the wife of his employer. The story ran nationally as a short wire item, several papers headlined it approvingly, and a Texas editor used it to charge Northern papers with a double standard on lynching.

According to an account credited to the Examiner, Scott had been hired by a Mr. Allison, who lived six miles from Brazil, to chop wood. That account alleged that he went to the house with his ax while Allison was away, assaulted Mrs. Allison in front of her three children, and left with a gold watch. Other papers named the husband as Joseph Allison, "a well-to-do farmer" in the eastern part of the county. An Omaha Bee special said Scott was captured at a place printed as "Marton, Ind.," and brought back to Brazil, where he was held in the Clay County jail.

The first Cincinnati Commercial dispatch said only that a party of masked men took Scott from the jail and lynched him. A special printed in the Memphis Public Ledger gave a fuller version, saying that 1000 men gathered at the jail, which stood in an isolated part of town, and that a guard held the crowd back. In that version, twenty men chosen by a leader demanded the keys and, when the jailer refused, battered the door open, secured the jailer, and took Scott from his cell. The Examiner account instead counted fifteen masked men who broke open the doors after the jailer refused the keys.

The Memphis special said Scott fought the men in the jail and again in the yard, cried "Murder!" and "Mercy!", and was badly bruised before being led to a tree near the jail. There, it said, ten men pulled on a rope thrown over a limb until he was dead, after which the crowd dispersed. The Examiner likewise said he was hanged to an adjacent tree.

The coroner cut the body down the next morning and took charge of it, according to the Memphis special, which added that no one could be found who had been there. Der Westbote expected that any attempt to identify the perpetrators would be futile, and no report of arrests, an inquest verdict, or indictments appears in the coverage.

Most papers carried the Commercial dispatch almost word for word under headings such as "Judge Lynch in Indiana" and "Lynched for an Outrage," and it was soon condensed into one-line roundup items from Washington to Nevada. The Chicago Tribune headed the item "A RAVISHER ROPED." and the Omaha Bee "A Just Retribution," while a Wisconsin weekly rendered the dispatch using a slur. The Memphis special was the most openly hostile, calling Scott a "villain" and scorning his cries as if "the worthless dog was entitled to anything like mercy or help."

The Dallas Daily Herald noted that the Chicago Inter-Ocean had called a South Carolina lynching a lack of civilization while printing this Indiana lynching without comment. The Herald concluded that to the Inter-Ocean nothing done in the South could be proper and "nothing that is wrong done in the north." The story was still circulating in January 1881, when a Mississippi weekly reprinted the Examiner account.

Reports differed on timing: most said Saturday night or early Sunday, while a St. Paul roundup said Friday night, the Examiner Saturday morning, and Der Westbote Sunday night. The first wire report alleged only an assault, but the Memphis special said Mrs. Allison had died a few hours before the hanging, and the Examiner said she died of the shock. An Arkansas roundup, by contrast, reported her death only as a rumor.

reader.title: Lynching of George Scott
bases: Masked men took Scott from the jail at Brazil, Indiana, where he was held on an assault accusation, and hanged him (A2, A8, A17).

Every report has Scott taken from jail by a party of masked men and hanged, with no legal process, over an accusation of outraging his employer's wife; the Memphis special counts twenty men in the jail party and the Examiner fifteen (A2, A17, A33).
The Cincinnati Commercial special, independent Brazil specials to the Omaha Bee and a Memphis paper, and an Examiner account agree on the jail seizure and hanging (A2, A8, A17, A33).
